script:
Hello, this is The Portfolio Podcast for MEME. Tuesday — here is your MEME recap. The portfolio closed down seven point seven five percent on the session. A broad, punishing selloff hit nearly every primary holding, and the damage was not evenly distributed.

Alphabet reported earnings Tuesday, and buried inside the results was a single line about capital expenditure that sent shockwaves through the entire optics and AI infrastructure trade. Optics names dropped double digits within hours.

No macro data was available for Tuesday's session. The selling pressure appeared concentrated in technology and AI-adjacent names, consistent with a rotation away from high-multiple growth following the Alphabet earnings print. The Nasdaq bore the brunt of the damage as traders reassessed the pace and duration of AI infrastructure spending.

The top story Tuesday belongs to Bloom Energy, and it cuts both ways. During regular trading, Bloom Energy fell eleven point three four percent — caught in the broad AI infrastructure selloff and still carrying weight from an early-July short-seller report. Then, after the close, the company reported second-quarter results that completely reframed the narrative. Revenue came in at one point zero seven billion dollars, surpassing one billion dollars for the first time in company history, representing a year-over-year gain of one hundred sixty-six percent. Non-GAAP earnings per share of seventy-eight cents beat analyst consensus estimates by ninety-one point eight percent. Full-year twenty twenty-six revenue guidance was raised to four point zero five billion dollars at the midpoint, coming in eight point two percent above what analysts had projected. Shares responded by jumping approximately eight percent in after-hours trading. The Brookfield Asset Management AI infrastructure partnership remains a key item for investors to monitor as follow-through details emerge.

Applied Optoelectronics was down nine point nine zero percent on the session. The move ties directly to Tuesday's dominant theme: Alphabet's earnings commentary triggered a sector-wide repricing of AI spending expectations, and optics names that had run triple digits year-to-date absorbed the sharpest corrections. According to reporting from Yahoo Finance, Applied Optoelectronics, Coherent, and Lumentum all fell in the range of nine to eleven percent as traders questioned the sustainability of the AI infrastructure buildout.

Turning to Redwire Corporation, which was down two point nine four percent on the session — the smallest decline among primary holdings Tuesday. A published comparison piece noted that Redwire generates three hundred thirty-five million dollars in annual revenue while a competing aerospace name trades at a valuation premium of one thousand seven hundred seventy times earnings. Dilution risk remains the key overhang to watch.

AST SpaceMobile was down two point nine nine percent on the session. The company confirmed it will launch BlueBird satellites eleven, twelve, and thirteen on August fifth, representing another step in its direct-to-device constellation buildout. Separately, the Federal Aviation Administration proposed environmental review waivers for commercial rocket launches, a structural regulatory tailwind for the broader sector. Watch execution on the August fifth launch closely.

Nebius Group was down nine point six eight percent on the session, placing it among the hardest-hit names in the portfolio Tuesday. No company-specific news was available; the move appears tied to the broader repricing of AI infrastructure and data center-adjacent technology names following the Alphabet print.

Over at Lumentum Holdings, the stock was down eight point four three percent on the session. Notably, it was Lumentum's own chief executive who flagged earlier in the day that an obscure semiconductor material shortage could become a larger constraint on AI infrastructure growth than memory — a forward-looking warning that did not cushion the stock from Tuesday's sector-wide selling.

TeraWulf was down four point nine five percent on the session. The name sits at the intersection of Bitcoin mining and AI compute infrastructure, and while no company-specific news drove Tuesday's move, the stock tracked the broader technology selloff without meaningful differentiation.

IREN Limited was down six point five zero percent on the session. Like TeraWulf, IREN operates in high-performance computing and digital infrastructure — a segment that sold off in sympathy with the broader AI trade Tuesday. No specific catalyst was reported.

Sandisk Corporation closed down fourteen point two five percent on the session, the steepest single-day decline across all primary holdings Tuesday. No company-specific news was identified as the direct driver, but storage and memory names broadly came under pressure as the Alphabet earnings report raised questions about the pace of data center capital deployment. Watch for any analyst commentary in the coming sessions.

Three items to watch in the next forty-eight hours. First, Bloom Energy will hold its earnings call to address guidance details and the Brookfield partnership — critical for assessing whether after-hours gains hold at Wednesday's open. Second, the Federal Reserve's policy meeting outcome is expected Wednesday, and any signal on rate trajectory carries direct implications for capital-intensive holdings across this portfolio. Third, monitor analyst response to Lumentum's CEO commentary on the semiconductor material supply constraint — any initiation or revision notes could move the broader optics complex.

This is The Portfolio Podcast for MEME. We will be back same time the next business day with tomorrow's news. Watch whether Bloom Energy's after-hours surge carries through to the regular session and whether the Alphabet-driven optics selloff finds a floor.
